title: Workers Just Went on Strike Against Humanoid Robots
hook: Hyundai's 40,000-member union walked out over the automaker's plan to bring in 25,000+ humanoid robots — likely the first labor strike ever aimed squarely at humanoid automation.
key_points: Hyundai's South Korean union held a three-day rolling strike with four-hour daily stoppages.
The target: Hyundai's plan to deploy 25,000+ Atlas humanoid robots across Hyundai and Kia plants by 2028.
Atlas is built by Hyundai-owned Boston Dynamics and starts at a Georgia factory in 2028.
Union demands: job-security guarantees, profit-linked bonuses, salaried pay, and final say over robot rollout.
The stoppage is estimated to have cut about 5,000 cars and roughly $135 million in sales revenue.
content_html: Robots taking factory jobs has been a talking point for decades. This week it became a picket line. Ars Technica reports Hyundai's 40,000-member South Korean union held a three-day rolling strike — four-hour work stoppages each day — explicitly targeting the automaker's plan to deploy more than 25,000 Atlas humanoid robots across Hyundai and Kia factories, likely the first labor strike ever aimed at humanoid robots specifically.
extra_html: Atlas is built by Boston Dynamics, which Hyundai owns, and it's due to start working at a Hyundai factory in Georgia in 2028 as part of a plan to build 30,000 units a year by then. Union leaders aren't objecting to automation in the abstract — they're worried about an "employment shock" as robots take on more line duties, and they want protections locked in before that happens: job-security guarantees built around the robots, bonuses that track Hyundai's profit margins, a shift from hourly pay to fixed salaries, and — most pointed of all — a formal agreement giving workers final say over any humanoid deployment. The stoppage is estimated to have cost around 5,000 cars and roughly $135 million in sales revenue, real leverage for a fight that's really about who controls the pace of automation, not whether it happens at all. It's a concrete preview of a negotiation more industries are likely to have as humanoid robots move from demos to actual production lines.

related.title: South Korea Bets $1 Trillion on Chips and Robots
related.hook: South Korea just committed roughly $1 trillion to memory chips, AI data centers, and mass-produced humanoid robots — a national wager that hardware, not just software, decides who leads AI.

related.title: GM's Robots and the 'Dark Factory'
related.hook: GM put robots into its flagship EV plant just after laying off 1,300 workers — and the autoworkers' union is warning of a 'dark factory' future where the lights stay off because nobody's there.

related.title: AI & Jobs
related.hook: AI is less likely to take your whole job than to take certain tasks within it. The pattern through history: tools reshape work faster than they erase it.

flashcards.prompt: What are Hyundai's union workers actually striking over?

choices.text: Hyundai's plan to deploy 25,000+ humanoid robots without agreed worker protections
A pay cut that already happened
The robots malfunctioning on the factory floor

flashcards.explanation_html: The strike targets the plan itself — workers want job-security guarantees and a say in the rollout before large-scale humanoid deployment begins.

flashcards.prompt: What is Atlas, and who makes it?
flashcards.back_html: Atlas is a humanoid robot built by Boston Dynamics, which Hyundai owns — it's set to start work at a Hyundai Georgia factory in 2028.

flashcards.prompt: What's one concrete demand the union is making before robots arrive?
flashcards.back_html: A formal agreement giving workers final say over any humanoid robotics deployment, alongside job-security guarantees and profit-linked bonuses.
